chunks: How a charge pump works. The question: How does a charge pump work?
A charge pump makes a higher (or negative) voltage using only switches and capacitors, with no inductor.
It charges a capacitor from the input, then rewires it so it sits on top of the input, which adds the two voltages. The output capacitor holds the result steady between pulses.
It works well for small currents, but the output sags as you draw more.
Imagine pouring water into a cup at floor level, then standing the cup on a stool and pouring it into a tank.
The stool adds height, so the water arrives higher than the floor level. The stool is the input voltage, and the cup is the flying capacitor.
The picture does not show the cost: each trip carries only a small amount, so the more you draw, the lower the tank level gets.
S1 and S2 closed. The animated current charges C fly from V in through two switches to ground. Meanwhile C out alone feeds the load (right-hand loop).
Flying capacitor: the capacitor that is charged, then moved to a new position in the circuit. Output capacitor: the capacitor that holds the output steady between pulses.
Phase: one of the two switch settings that alternate every cycle. Output resistance ( R out ): how much the output sags per amp of load.
Doubler: a charge pump with an ideal output of 2 volts in .
Take a doubler with a 3 volts input. In phase one the flying capacitor charges to 3 volts.
In phase two it is stacked on the 3 volts input, so the output is 3 plus 3 equals 6 volts. Under load, say 20 milliamps with R out equals 8 ohms, the output sags by 0.

In phase two it's re-wired in series with the input and dumps its charge into the output capacitor, so the output is about 2 volts in .
